scenes.title: A confirmation is only as good as its question
scenes.body: "Allow delete_task(task_id=1)?" makes people click yes without reading. "Delete task 1. Pay rent (high, due 2026-11-05)?" shows **exactly** what will happen. Ask for every dangerous call, describe it in plain words, and treat silence as **no**.

scenes.title: Pause and try: choose the level

items.q: How do you make a tool-using agent safe?
items.a: **Least privilege** (only the tools it needs), permission levels, **validate every input**, timeouts, and **human approval** for irreversible actions, with clear confirmation text and a log of decisions.
items.trap: "Tell the model in the prompt to be careful." Prompts guide; only code enforces.

items.q: Where should the human-approval check live?
items.a: In **your code**, between validation and execution, so it runs no matter what the model says. The model can be told about it, but never relied on to enforce it.
items.trap: Asking the model to ask the user for permission in its reply.

scenes.question: Why does the policy validate the input before asking the human?
options: So a human only approves a real, well-formed action
scenes.explain: Asking a person to approve an invalid or impossible call wastes their attention and teaches them to click yes.

items.text: Least privilege: only the tools and powers the job needs
read always; write unless read-only; danger needs a human yes
Validate first, then ask, with a clear question
Enforce in code, never only in the prompt

captions.text: So far, every valid tool call simply runs.
That's fine for listing tasks.
It's not fine for deleting your data, sending an email, or paying a bill.
In this lesson you'll give every tool a permission level, add a read-only mode, and
make the agent ask a human before anything dangerous happens.
You'll explain the principle of least privilege for agents.
Sort tools into read, write, and danger.
Block writes in a read-only mode.
And ask a human before every dangerous action.
Let's start with an idea security engineers use everywhere: least privilege.
Think of a hotel key card.
It doesn't open every door in the building.
It opens your room, for your stay.
If you lose it, the damage is small.
For agents, least privilege means: give the agent only the tools and powers it needs
for this job, and nothing more.
Why does this matter so much for agents?
Because a model can misunderstand a request, and a user, or text inside a document,
can try to trick it into doing something harmful.
Permissions limit the damage, even when the model gets it wrong.
Our project uses three levels.
Read: list tasks and search notes.
These are always allowed, because looking never changes anything.
Write: add task, complete task, and add note.
These change data, so they're allowed, unless the agent runs in read-only mode.
And danger: delete task.
Deleting can't be undone, so a human must approve every single call.
Here's the policy.
It holds the context, a read-only flag, and ask human: a function that asks a person
a yes or no question.
If there's nobody to ask, it's None, and dangerous calls are denied.
It also keeps a log of every decision.
The check runs before every call.
Read tools return straight away: allowed.
In read-only mode, any other tool is blocked, with a clear reason the model can pass
on to the user.
For danger tools, we build a clear question, using the tool's confirm function.
For delete task, it says which task, by number and title, so the human knows exactly
what they're approving.
Then we ask.
Anything other than yes means no.
The decision is logged, and if it's declined, the model gets a tool error that says:
the user declined, don't retry it.
Let's try four calls.
In read-only mode, listing tasks is allowed.
But completing a task is blocked, and nothing changes.
Now a dangerous call.
The policy asks the human: delete task one, pay rent?
This human says no, so the call is declined, and the task stays.
And when the human says yes, only then does the delete actually run.
The order of these checks matters.
First, does the tool exist?
If not, error.
Second, is the input valid?
We never ask a human to approve nonsense.
Third, for a delete, does the task exist?
We need it to write a clear question.
Fourth, the permission check, which asks the human only for danger tools.
And fifth, run the tool with its timeout.
Now in the real agent.
An empty store, and two tasks added, in one turn.
Delete task one.
The agent stops and asks.
Here I pipe in the answer no, so you can see it in the recording.
The delete is declined, and the task is safe.
And in read-only mode, even adding a task is blocked.
That's a good default for an agent that should only answer questions about your
data.
One warning about confirmations.
A question like, allow delete task, task ID one, teaches people to click yes without
reading.
A good question shows exactly what will happen, in plain words: delete task one, pay
rent, high priority.
Ask for every dangerous call, not just the first, and treat no answer as a no.
Pause and choose a permission level for each of these tools.
One.
Get weather, for a city.
Two.
Rename task.
Three.
Send email.
Get weather is read: it only looks.
Rename task is write: it changes data, but it's easy to undo.
Send email is danger: once it's sent, you can't take it back, so a human should
approve every one.
Interview corner.
How do you make a tool-using agent safe?
Least privilege, so only the tools it needs.
Permission levels.
Validate every input.
Timeouts.
And human approval for actions that can't be undone, with a clear confirmation and a
log of every decision.
The trap: saying, tell the model in the prompt to be careful.
Prompts guide the model.
Only code enforces the rules.
Follow-up: where should the approval check live?
In your code, between validation and execution, so it runs no matter what the model
says.
You can tell the model about it, but never rely on the model to enforce it.
The trap: asking the model to ask the user for permission in its reply.
Quick check.
Why does the policy validate the input before asking the human?
So a human only ever approves a real, well-formed action.
Asking about nonsense wastes their attention, and teaches them to click yes without
reading.
Recap.
Least privilege: only the tools and powers the job needs.
Read is always allowed, write unless read-only, and danger needs a human yes.
Validate first, then ask, with a clear question.
And enforce it in code, never only in the prompt.
You now know every idea in this module.
Next lesson, we put them together, and build the personal productivity agent.
